articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has released its Children’s Services Directorate Plan for the first quarter of the 2026-27 financial year, outlining key objectives and initiatives for local children's services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has published its Children’s Services Directorate Plan for the first quarter of the 2026-27 financial year. The document outlines the council's strategic objectives aimed at improving services for children and families in the borough.

Key priorities include enhancing educational outcomes, safeguarding children, and promoting well-being among young residents. This plan serves as a framework for the council's activities and resource allocation in the upcoming year.

The publication reflects the council's commitment to transparency and accountability, ensuring stakeholders are informed about the direction of children's services in Rochdale.

Residents can access the full document through the Rochdale Borough Council's official website for more detailed information on the specific initiatives outlined in the plan.

articles.title: Dr Helen Palmer Appointed New Chair of Rochdale Creates
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Creates has appointed Dr Helen Palmer as the new independent chair of its Cultural Compact, bringing over 30 years of experience in culture and heritage to the role.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Creates has appointed Dr Helen Palmer as the new independent chair of Rochdale Borough’s Cultural Compact. Dr Palmer brings more than 30 years of experience in culture, heritage, placemaking, tourism, and partnership development at local, regional, and national levels.

Dr Palmer has a long-standing connection with Rochdale, having collaborated with local cultural organisations and partners, including Touchstones Rochdale and Rochdale Council. Most recently, she worked with the Rochdale Development Agency, providing marketing and communications training for the borough’s creative and cultural sector.

In her role as chair, Dr Palmer will provide independent leadership for Rochdale Creates, supporting partners in delivering the borough’s shared cultural vision. Her focus will be on strengthening collaboration across sectors and ensuring that culture continues to play a central role in Rochdale’s regeneration, wellbeing, community pride, and economic growth.

Rochdale Creates, established in 2022, is a partnership that unites cultural organisations, artists, educators, businesses, community groups, and public sector partners. The Compact aims to champion culture as a driver of regeneration and economic opportunity, and Dr Palmer's leadership is expected to enhance its governance and long-term sustainability.

articles.title: Zambrero Opens First UK Franchise Location in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Zambrero has launched its first UK franchise location in Rochdale, marking a significant milestone for the brand's expansion in the country.
articles.content_html:
Zambrero, the Australian fast-casual restaurant chain, has opened its first UK franchise location in Rochdale. This opening is notable as it is the first to be supported by a Development Agent, highlighting the brand's commitment to expanding its presence in the UK market.

The new restaurant aims to offer a menu focused on fresh, healthy Mexican cuisine, with a strong emphasis on sustainability and social responsibility. Zambrero is known for its 'Plate 4 Plate' initiative, which provides a meal to someone in need for every meal sold.

The opening of this franchise is expected to create local jobs and contribute to the community's economy. It also reflects the growing demand for diverse dining options in Rochdale.

As Zambrero continues to expand, further openings in other locations across the UK may follow.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Wins Legal Battle Over Hopwood Hall Sale
articles.excerpt: American actor Hopwood DePree has lost a court case against Rochdale Council regarding the sale of the historic Hopwood Hall, which he claimed ancestral ties to.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has emerged victorious in a legal dispute with American actor Hopwood DePree over the sale of Hopwood Hall, a grade II-listed building dating back to the 1400s. DePree argued that the council acted illegally by refusing to sell him the property, which he claims ancestral links to.

The dispute began after DePree signed an exclusivity agreement with the council in 2017, allowing him to acquire Hopwood Hall for £1. However, the agreement stipulated that he must demonstrate the ability to refurbish the entire hall. The council contended that DePree failed to meet this requirement, despite a successful change of use application in 2022 to convert part of the hall into a wedding and hospitality venue.

In 2024, the council decided not to renew the exclusivity agreement, citing an independent financial consultant's assessment that DePree's proposed business model would be loss-making and unable to secure further funding. This assessment played a crucial role in the council's decision to refuse the sale.

The outcome of this legal battle means that the council retains control over Hopwood Hall, which has been the subject of restoration efforts by DePree and his volunteers. The future of the historic property remains uncertain as the council continues to explore options for its preservation and potential use.

articles.title: Ofsted Inspection Report Published for Alice Marie Galvin
articles.excerpt: Ofsted has released a new inspection report for Alice Marie Galvin, detailing the findings and rating awarded to the childcare provider in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Ofsted has published a new inspection report for Alice Marie Galvin, a childcare provider in Rochdale, dated 1 October 2026. The report outlines the findings from the recent inspection and includes the rating awarded to the provider.

Settings registered on the Early Years Register are typically inspected at least once within a four-year period. However, inspections may occur more frequently if there are concerns. Newly registered settings are inspected within 18 months of their registration date. The report provides insights into the quality of care and education provided by Galvin, as well as compliance with the latest requirements set by the Department for Education.

Parents and guardians can access the report to understand the quality of care their children receive. Additionally, they can subscribe to alerts to be notified when new reports for this provider are published. Ofsted encourages families to search and compare other childminders in the area to make informed decisions about childcare.

For further information or inquiries, individuals can visit the Ofsted contact page. The report is part of Ofsted's commitment to ensuring high standards in early years education and care, which is crucial for the development of young children in the community.

articles.title: Supermarkets Urged to Address Litter Issues Along Rochdale Canal
articles.excerpt: A litter picking group has called on Aldi, Morrisons, and Tesco to take action after repeatedly retrieving trolleys from the Rochdale canal, highlighting ongoing litter problems in the area.
articles.content_html:
A litter picking group in Failsworth has urged Aldi, Morrisons, and Tesco to take action regarding the increasing number of supermarket trolleys found in the Rochdale canal. The group, Clean Up Failsworth Canal, has been active for over 13 years, conducting monthly clean-ups along the canal, where they regularly encounter discarded trolleys, flytipped rubbish, and other litter.

On September 20, the group collected 22 bags of rubbish, 26 nitrous oxide canisters, and 17 supermarket trolleys from the canal. Sandra Ball, a local councillor representing Failsworth West for Reform UK, expressed frustration over the ongoing issue, stating that the supermarkets need to 'get their act together' to prevent trolleys from being dumped in the water. She noted that the problem has persisted for years, with some clean-up sessions yielding as many as 20 trolleys.

The litter picking efforts are supported by Oldham Council and the Canal and River Trust, with around 90 volunteers participating in the initiative. Despite their hard work, Ball described the situation as 'disheartening', as litter reappears almost immediately after clean-ups. Local resident Lesley Halliday, who participates in the clean-ups with her grandson, echoed these sentiments, highlighting the frustration of seeing litter reappear shortly after it has been removed.

In response to the concerns, a spokesperson for Morrisons stated that they make efforts to retrieve abandoned trolleys as soon as they are made aware of them. Tesco also encouraged customers to return their trolleys and mentioned that they employ a specialist company to handle abandoned trolleys. The ongoing litter issues in the canal raise concerns about the local environment and the impact on community efforts to maintain a clean and pleasant area.

articles.title: Whitworth Man Sentenced to Two Years and Eight Months for Attempted Robbery with Imitation Firearm
articles.excerpt: Lee Stretton, 45, from Whitworth, has been sentenced to two years and eight months in prison for attempting to rob a man using a fake gun in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A 45-year-old man from Whitworth has been sentenced to two years and eight months in prison for attempted robbery while in possession of an imitation firearm. Lee Stretton, of Westgate Close, appeared before Preston Crown Court after being charged with one count of possessing an imitation firearm and attempted robbery.

The incident occurred on June 2, when Stretton attempted to rob a man of £1,000 while brandishing a fake handgun. The court heard that Stretton's actions were premeditated, and he posed a significant threat to the victim during the attempted robbery.

In addition to the prison sentence, the court highlighted the seriousness of using an imitation firearm in the commission of a crime, which can instil fear and distress in victims. The judge noted that such behaviour would not be tolerated in the community.

Stretton's conviction serves as a reminder of the legal consequences of engaging in violent crime, even when no real weapon is involved. The case underscores the importance of public safety and the judicial system's commitment to addressing such offences.

articles.excerpt: Zambrero has launched its first UK restaurant in Rochdale, creating six jobs and offering a diverse menu. The site opened on 25 September 2026 on Mellor Street, near the town centre.
articles.content_html:
Zambrero has opened its first UK restaurant in Rochdale, marking a significant milestone for the brand as it expands its presence in the country. The new site, located on Mellor Street, officially opened on 25 September 2026 and has created six new jobs for the local community.

The restaurant features seating for 18 customers and offers a variety of dining options, including dine-in, takeaway, and delivery services. The menu includes popular items such as burritos, bowls, tacos, nachos, and quesadillas, with vegetarian, vegan, and halal options available to cater to diverse dietary preferences.

The opening of this site was supported by Zambrero’s Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire Development Agents, Damian Bennett and Dawn Catherall, who provided essential local guidance and recommendations to the franchise partner. The restaurant is operated by a multi-brand franchise operator who has plans to open additional Zambrero locations in the future.

This development is expected to enhance the local dining scene and provide residents with more options for healthy and convenient meals. The restaurant's proximity to Rochdale town centre and local colleges may also attract students and visitors, contributing to the area's economic growth.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Wins High Court Case Against Hopwood DePree
articles.excerpt: An American man has lost his legal bid to take ownership of Hopwood Hall in Middleton for £1 after a High Court ruling.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

02:08, 01 October 2026

An American man has lost his legal bid to take ownership of Hopwood Hall in Middleton for £1 after a High Court ruling.

Rochdale Council has successfully defended its ownership of Hopwood Hall in Middleton after a High Court judge ruled against Hopwood DePree, who sought to acquire the Grade II-listed mansion for £1. DePree, an American actor and filmmaker, claimed ancestral ties to the property and argued that a 2017 agreement with the council entitled him to purchase the hall following the securing of planning permission for its restoration and redevelopment.

Judge David Hodge KC found that the conditions necessary for the transfer of ownership had not been met. Despite its current dilapidated state, the court noted that Hopwood Hall is among the top 10% of most important listed buildings in England. DePree's plans included transforming the hall into a wedding venue, hotel, and visitor attractions to revive the historic site.

In 2022, Rochdale Council decided against transferring ownership to DePree and subsequently barred him and a group of volunteers from accessing the site. DePree expressed his disappointment following the ruling, stating that he had hoped to restore the hall to its former glory.

The council's victory in this case reinforces its commitment to preserving the historic significance of Hopwood Hall, which remains a key landmark in the area. The ruling also means that the council will retain control over any future developments concerning the property.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: A small, stubbornly local verb that names the familiar ankle-twist — where it comes from, how local it really is, and what dialect research tells us.
articles.summary: A small, stubbornly local verb that names the familiar ankle-twist — where it comes from, how local it really is, and what dialect research tells us.
articles.body:
Anyone from parts of Rochdale will recognise the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” In local use, cruckle (sometimes heard and written crookle) most commonly names that sudden roll or twist of the foot you can usually walk off but will still wince about. It is a compact, expressive verb and — crucially for dialect researchers — one that locals readily name when talking about the town’s speech.

Where the word comes from

Cruckle sits in a larger family of northern English and Scots dialect words meaning to bend, crouch, stoop or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect lexicography records forms such as crookle and crookl(e) with senses like “to make crooked, to bend, to stoop.” Those older entries fit the meaning Rochdalians use today: a bending or awkward movement of the foot or body. The frequentative or diminutive suffix ‑le (present in many dialect verbs) and the root crook/krug (suggesting a hook or bend) help explain how crook → crookle → cruckle developed as a natural dialect shape.

Scots dialect dictionaries record closely related forms (cruggle, kruggle, krukel and cruckle) meaning to crouch or huddle, showing that the same verbal pattern has a wide historical reach across the north of Britain rather than being invented in Rochdale overnight.

How strongly it’s tied to Rochdale

People in and around Greater Manchester often treat cruckle as a Rochdale‑flavoured word. That perception is borne out in recent perceptual dialect research: a 2024 draw‑a‑map study of folk labels for Greater Manchester speech collected comments from local residents and recorded words people used to describe particular places’ speech. One respondent’s list of keywords describing Rochdale included “broad, flat, cruckle, guinnel,” showing that cruckle is part of the way some locals and neighbouring residents characterise Rochdale speech.

Two points follow from this. First, cruckle is not uniquely Rochdale in the sense of being unprecedented elsewhere — cognate forms appear across northern dialect sources — but second, modern speakers strongly associate the form cruckle with Rochdale in ordinary folk talk. In short: historically widespread roots, locally strong identity.

What dialect research tells us

Two kinds of evidence are useful. Historical lexicography (the English Dialect Dictionary and related sources) documents the older verb family and its meanings; linguistic geography and perceptual dialectology show how people today attach words to places. Together they give a plausible account: cruckle is a predictable local survival and reshaping of a long‑standing northern dialect verb, and contemporary perception maps show Rochdale as one of the places where the word still figures in local descriptions.

A word of caution on origins and legends

The word also crops up in occasional local place‑name commentary (for example a “Cruckles Well” recorded in historic notes for other towns) and in popular lists of regional words. Those claims can be interesting but are often speculative: where a place‑name appears to link to an old dialect word, that link is a plausible hypothesis rather than a proven etymology unless supported by dated documentary evidence. In other words, treat folktales and place‑name suggestions as tradition or interpretation, not as the same thing as documented lexical history.

Why it matters locally

Small words like cruckle matter because they carry local identity. They are ways people name shared experience (that sudden ankle‑twist) and, in doing so, mark membership of a place. Dialect scholars treat such words as data: they help map the geography of speech, the memory of older forms, and how communities talk about their own language. For Rochdale, cruckle is a neat example of a living piece of the borough’s verbal landscape — historically rooted, regionally connected, and distinctly local in everyday perception.

If you want to follow up

Authoritative historical lexica (the English Dialect Dictionary and Scots dialect dictionaries) show the older family of forms; recent perceptual research in the Journal of Linguistic Geography (2024) documents cruckle as one of the folk‑terms people associate with Rochdale. If a fuller historical proof for any single place‑name link is required, that should be sought in dated local records or place‑name studies rather than in modern recollection.

Bottom line: cruckle is not a made‑up novelty — it’s a local survival of an old northern verb pattern — and while related forms exist elsewhere, local speakers and recent research both show that the word is especially, and recognisably, Rochdalian today.

articles.title: Planning Permission Refused for New Home at Standrings House in Norden
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has refused planning permission for a new four-bedroom home on the grounds of the historic Standrings House, citing concerns over the impact on the Grade-II listed property.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for planning permission to build a four-bedroom home on the grounds of Standrings House, a Grade-II listed building located at the corner of Bagslate Moor Road and Greenview Drive in Norden. The application was submitted by Jonathan Mulroy, who sought to construct the new house and a car port at the rear of the historic farmhouse, which dates back to 1791 and was originally a moorland farmstead before being converted into a home in the 1930s.

The planning documents, prepared by Paul Butler Associates on behalf of Mark Bell Architects Ltd, proposed creating a separate plot in the south-eastern corner of the garden, with access from Greenview Drive. The plans included the installation of new gates that would match the existing character of the property and its surroundings. However, the council's planning committee ultimately decided against the proposal, although specific reasons for the refusal have not been disclosed in the available records.

Standrings House is significant not only for its age but also for its architectural features, which contribute to the local heritage. The refusal of this planning application highlights the council's commitment to preserving the integrity of historic sites within the borough. The decision may also reflect broader concerns regarding development in areas surrounding listed buildings, where the potential impact on the character and setting of such properties is carefully considered.

As a result of this decision, there are currently no plans for new development on the site. The refusal may prompt the applicant to reconsider their approach or submit a revised proposal in the future. Local residents and heritage advocates may view this outcome as a positive step towards maintaining the historical character of the area.

articles.title: High Court Rules Against Hopwood DePree in Ownership Dispute Over Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: The High Court has ruled that Rochdale Council acted fairly in its decision not to transfer ownership of Hopwood Hall to Hopwood DePree, a descendant of the original owners.
articles.content_html:
The High Court in Manchester has ruled that Rochdale Council did not act unfairly in its decision to deny ownership of Hopwood Hall to Hopwood DePree, a descendant of the family that built the historic property in the 1420s. The ruling concluded a two-day trial concerning an exclusivity agreement that had been terminated by the council, which currently owns the Grade II-listed hall.

Following the court's decision, DePree expressed disappointment, stating that it was a significant setback for both his community and heritage rescue groups across the UK. He indicated that his legal team is considering their options for further action and will closely monitor the council's plans for the future of Hopwood Hall.

Hopwood Hall, which is located adjacent to Hopwood Hall College, has a rich history, having been owned by the Hopwood family until 1922. The property was sold two decades later and has since been occupied by various temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who used it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. The hall has since fallen into disrepair and was acquired by Rochdale Council, which aims to restore it.

The ruling has implications for the future of Hopwood Hall, as the council continues its efforts to preserve the building for community use. The next steps for both the council and DePree remain to be seen as discussions about the hall's future continue.

articles.title: Hopwood Hall College Graduate Celebrates Wedding and Graduation on Same Day
articles.excerpt: Kelly Simpson, a graduate of Hopwood Hall College, wore her wedding dress to collect her qualification just hours after her wedding, during the Class of 2026 graduation ceremony at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
A graduate from Hopwood Hall College celebrated a unique milestone by wearing her wedding dress to her graduation ceremony just hours after getting married. Kelly Simpson, 44, joined fellow graduates at Rochdale Town Hall on September 30, 2026, where family and friends gathered to support the Class of 2026 during the Higher Education Graduation and Awards Ceremony.

Simpson, who completed a Foundation Degree in Early Years, expressed her joy at combining two significant life events into one day. "It felt very extravagant to graduate in my wedding dress – but why not?" she said. She added that one of her lecturers even attended her wedding, highlighting the close-knit community at the college.

The graduation ceremony featured students of various ages receiving their qualifications, with Emily Mills, who earned a BSc in Zoo Science and Wildlife Conservation, delivering the graduates' address. The event was marked by cheers and applause as students took to the stage to collect their certificates, celebrating their academic achievements alongside personal milestones.

This year's graduation not only recognised the hard work of the students but also showcased the supportive environment fostered at Hopwood Hall College, where students are encouraged to celebrate their achievements in unique ways. The ceremony took place in the Great Hall of Rochdale Town Hall, a historic venue that added to the significance of the occasion.

articles.title: Finalists Announced for Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026 finalists have been revealed, recognising 25 individuals and organisations for their contributions to equality and inclusion in the borough.
articles.content_html:
The finalists for the Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026 have been announced, showcasing 25 individuals, organisations, and community initiatives shortlisted for their efforts in promoting equality and inclusion across the borough. The awards, managed by the Kashmir Youth Project (KYP) since 2012, celebrate those who contribute to a more inclusive and connected Rochdale.

This year's finalists were selected from over 120 nominations, highlighting the diverse range of people and organisations making a positive impact in the community. The shortlist includes representatives from community organisations, educational institutions, health professionals, public-sector partnerships, and local employers, all working to champion equality, diversity, and inclusion.

The winners will be revealed at the Rochdale Diversity Awards ceremony on Friday, October 23, at Rochdale Town Hall. The event will bring together community leaders, organisations, businesses, and residents to celebrate excellence in these areas. The awards are supported by various sponsors and partners committed to promoting equality and diversity in the borough.

Zulf Ahmed, Chief Executive Officer of KYP, expressed pride in announcing the finalists, stating, "We are incredibly proud to announce the finalists for the Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026." The awards ceremony promises to be a significant event in recognising the contributions of those dedicated to fostering an inclusive community.

articles.title: Rochdale Businesses Encouraged to Support Christmas Toy Appeal for Local Children
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council is calling on local businesses to contribute to this year’s Christmas Toy Appeal, aiming to provide gifts for children living in poverty across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is appealing to employers and businesses in the borough to support this year’s Christmas Toy Appeal, which aims to ensure that children living in poverty receive gifts this festive season. The appeal, organised by the council’s staff charity in partnership with Rochdale Football Club, Rochdale Riverside, and Your Trust, has been a vital source of support for families in need since its inception in 2013.

Last year, the appeal saw a record number of donations, with over 10,000 toys and gifts collected, benefiting more than 2,700 children. The success of the initiative highlights the community's commitment to helping those less fortunate during the holiday season. Rochdale Council noted that the appeal is set to return soon, and they are actively seeking contributions from local businesses to help maintain this momentum.

Businesses can assist in various ways, whether through direct donations of toys and gifts or by encouraging their employees to participate. The council emphasised the importance of community involvement in making Christmas special for all children, particularly those facing financial hardships.

As the launch date for this year’s appeal approaches, local businesses are encouraged to consider how they can contribute to this meaningful cause. Further details on how to get involved will be shared by the council in the coming weeks.
